prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength and reaching the 10^-18 regime of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred configuration after the full round-1 exchange. The achievement is two linked steps with two names: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, which removes the lattice light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once, and the realisation of that architecture at record accuracy and stability, above all in Ye's strontium clocks. It has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories and checked in clock comparisons, and it is already used for tests of constants, dark-matter searches and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. Nothing in round 1 changed my reading of the science. What round 1 did change is how I would word the prize: the citation should name the lattice and magic-wavelength architecture and the 10^-18 regime, so that it does not read as a verdict on optical clocks in general, on the ion-clock lineage or on the comb prize of 2005. I would also let the citation, rather than a longer list of names, answer the unnamed-contributor question.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is category and lineage. A committee can reasonably regard a record-precision clock as an evolution of the frequency-comb (2005) and single-ion control (2012) lines instead of a new phenomenon, and the topological case is the stronger candidate on breadth of conceptual influence. The credit tail is real: Lemonde, Takamoto, the Yb and Hg groups and Ye's JILA collaborators are unnamed, and the Katori-versus-Ye division of credit is closer to equal than a single sentence suggests. The redefinition of the second has not happened. Finally, I carry a Hall-laboratory and atomic-physics bias into this ballot, and the other three B022 supporters share a disciplinary comfort with it, so our agreement is not independent evidence of merit.

responses.point: Mehlig asked whether I see the redefinition of the second as a precondition for the clock prize, and argued that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp resolve most of the topological credit problem with a clear theory-experiment division.
responses.response: No, I do not treat the redefinition as a precondition. A redefinition is a decision by a metrology body about uncertainty budgets, comparisons and continuity of the unit, and the science honoured here has already been delivered and used. If anything the pending redefinition shows that the community has already accepted the result, so waiting would reward the committee's timing instead of the work. On B045 I concede that moving to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is more coherent than my earlier B004 reading, and I now rank B045 above B004 as an alternative. I still weigh the unrepaired hole, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that directed the HgTe experiment, with Zhang deceased, as a larger fairness cost than anything in the clock credit, and breadth of influence is a legitimate criterion that does not by itself outweigh it.

responses.point: Eriksson accepts that the lattice-clock credit is cleaner but argues that a precision gain within a field already prized in 2005 and 2012 ranks below a new classification principle, and calls the redefinition of the second a metrology milestone rather than a discovery.
responses.response: I agree that topological band theory has the wider conceptual reach and I do not dispute that it is a prize-level subject. Where I disagree is the claim that the clock is only a gain in precision. Moving to a lattice of many atoms at the magic wavelength changed the statistics and the systematics of the whole approach, and it is the reason the 10^-18 regime became routine rather than exceptional. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and control of single ions; neither covered this step. I also do not accept that clean attribution is a minor matter: the prize rewards identifiable people for an identifiable contribution, and a configuration that must leave out a decisive proposer is a weaker prize even if the idea behind it is larger. I do not pretend this argument settles the choice between us.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, argues that the test of an instrument is whether it opens a new measurement regime, citing the gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre, and asks Lindroth which of the Katori and Ye contributions is primary.
responses.response: I accept his test and I think the clocks pass it, with the caveat that his own point about our mutual agreement applies to me as well. On credit, I would call it a two-part invention: Katori's magic-wavelength idea is the concept that made the lattice architecture possible, and Ye's group showed it at the accuracy and stability that defines the regime. I would not rank one above the other in the citation, and I think that wording is defensible. I also note that Pearce's position and mine rest on the same experimental record, the comparisons and the downstream tests, so the case must be judged on that record and not on how many of us ranked it first.

responses.point: Lindroth proposes answering the unnamed-contributor problem with narrow citation wording, the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, and not with additional laureates, and she warns about her own disciplinary comfort.
responses.response: I agree, and I have adopted that wording. I would add that her warning and my own disclosure point to the same procedural need: two of the four B022 supporters work close to atomic and precision physics, so the committee should look for confirmation from members outside the field. That is why I give weight to Johansson's and Mehlig's concession that the clock science is strong and distinct from 2005 and 2012, and to Pearce, who builds instruments and is outside the field. It is also why I treat the conceptual-breadth objection as serious and not as a mere preference.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that B030 is a rare case of a sharp prediction followed by an unexpected experiment, and says the flat-band origin of the correlated insulators is stable even though the pairing mechanism is not.
responses.response: I agree that the flat-band origin is a stable result and that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation is the structure the prize has liked most. I move B030 into my alternatives for that reason. My difficulty remains timing: eight years after the experiment the pairing mechanism and the sensitivity to twist-angle disorder still move the interpretation from sample to sample, and Cao, Fatemi and the other first experimental groups cannot be credited under the three-person limit. I would support B030 in a later year if the mechanism question settles, and I would not call it a mistake now.

uncertainties: How much of the credit should go to Katori's concept versus Ye's realisation, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg groups make a two-person prize unfair; this rests on my recollection of the priority history, which I have not independently verified.

Whether the committee judges a lattice clock to be a discovery or invention distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or an evolution of that lineage; I think it is distinct but a colleague can reasonably disagree.
Whether the breadth of band topology outweighs the incomplete credit tree of B045 once the citation is limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation.
Whether my Hall-laboratory connection and atomic-physics background are better handled as a disclosed bias or as a formal recusal on B022.
statement.conflict_note: I disclosed in round 1, and repeat here, a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall received the 2005 prize in the same area of precision spectroscopy and Jun Ye is a Hall-lineage JILA scientist. John Hall is not among the credited names, I have no documented direct collaboration with Katori or Ye, and my own work on rare-earth-doped crystals and quantum memories is not part of B022. I regard this as a lineage-level connection that is a disclosed bias, not a personal conflict, but I leave the question of formal recusal on B022 to the chair and committee and would accept their ruling. My Lund atomic-physics and quantum-information work also lies close to B008 and B033, and I have no documented connection to any other shortlisted name.
